section.title: Shimei Curses David
section.sectionRationale: As David flees, he meets Ziba with provisions and a slander against Mephibosheth, then Shimei, a man of Saul's house, who pelts him with stones and curses, calling him a man of blood. David refuses to let Abishai kill Shimei, submitting to the possibility that the LORD is behind the cursing and hoping God may repay him with good. Meanwhile Absalom enters Jerusalem, publicly takes David's concubines on Ahithophel's advice, fulfilling Nathan's word. The movement shows David humbled under reproach and God's judgment unfolding, even as David's shrewd counter-plan quietly proceeds.
section.thesis: In his lowest hour David absorbs a bitter cursing without retaliation, submitting to God's hand even in Shimei's abuse and hoping for God's mercy, while Absalom's public seizure of the royal concubines fulfills the very judgment Nathan announced, so that humility under reproach and the outworking of God's word stand side by side.
section.frameNote: Three beats: Ziba's provisions and slander against Mephibosheth, verses 1 to 4; Shimei's cursing and David's humble restraint, verses 5 to 14; and Absalom in Jerusalem taking the concubines on Ahithophel's counsel, verses 15 to 23.

verses.text: When David had gone a little beyond the summit, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth was there to meet him. He had a pair of saddled donkeys loaded with two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred clusters of raisins, a hundred summer fruits, and a skin of wine.

“Why do you have these?” asked the king. Ziba replied, “The donkeys are for the king’s household to ride, the bread and summer fruit are for the young men to eat, and the wine is to refresh those who become exhausted in the wilderness.”

“Where is your master’s grandson?” asked the king. And Ziba answered, “Indeed, he is staying in Jerusalem, for he has said, ‘Today, the house of Israel will restore to me the kingdom of my grandfather.’”
So the king said to Ziba, “All that belongs to Mephibosheth is now yours!” “I humbly bow before you,” said Ziba. “May I find favor in your eyes, my lord the king!”

units.label: Shimei curses David
units.note: let him curse, the LORD has told him

verses.text: As King David approached Bahurim, a man from the family of the house of Saul was just coming out. His name was Shimei son of Gera, and as he approached, he kept yelling out curses.
He threw stones at David and at all the servants of the king, though the troops and all the mighty men were on David’s right and left.
And as he yelled {{qalal|curses}}, Shimei said, “Get out, get out, you worthless man of bloodshed!

The LORD has paid you back for all the blood of the house of Saul, in whose place you have reigned, and the LORD has delivered the kingdom into the hand of your son Absalom. See, you have come to ruin because you are a man of bloodshed!”
Then Abishai son of Zeruiah said to the king, “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and cut off his head!”
But the king replied, “What have I to do with you, O sons of Zeruiah? If he curses me because the LORD told him, ‘Curse David,’ who can ask, ‘Why did you do this?’”

Then David said to Abishai and to all his servants, “Behold, my own son, my own flesh and blood, seeks my life. How much more, then, this Benjamite! Leave him alone and let him curse me, for the LORD has told him so.
Perhaps the LORD will see my {{oni|affliction}} and repay me with good for the cursing I receive today.”
So David and his men proceeded along the road as Shimei went along the ridge of the hill opposite him. As Shimei went, he yelled curses, threw stones, and flung dust at David.
Finally, the king and all the people with him arrived, exhausted. And there he refreshed himself.

units.label: Absalom takes the concubines
units.note: in the sight of all Israel

verses.text: Then Absalom and all the men of Israel came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel was with him.
And David’s friend Hushai the Archite went to Absalom and said to him, “Long live the king! Long live the king!”
“Is this the loyalty you show your friend?” Absalom replied. “Why did you not go with your friend?”
“Not at all,” Hushai answered. “For the one chosen by the LORD, by this people, and by all the men of Israel, his I will be, and with him I will remain.
Furthermore, whom should I serve if not his son? As I served in your father’s presence, so also I will serve in yours.”
Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, “Give me counsel. What should we do?”

Ahithophel replied, “Sleep with your father’s concubines, whom he has left to take care of the palace. When all Israel hears that you have become a stench to your father, then the hands of all who are with you will be strengthened.”
So they pitched a tent for Absalom on the roof, and he slept with his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel.
Now in those days the advice of Ahithophel was like the consultation of the word of God. Such was the regard that both David and Absalom had for Ahithophel’s advice.

qalal.gloss: To curse, to treat as light, trifling, or of no account, to revile. Shimei relentlessly qalal, curses, David, calling him a man of blood and declaring his fall God's judgment. To curse the LORD's anointed was a grave offense, yet David bears it, wondering whether the LORD Himself stands behind the reviling and might turn it to good.

oni.gloss: Affliction, misery, humiliation, the suffering of the lowly and oppressed. David hopes the LORD will look on his oni, his affliction, and repay him with good for the cursing. The word ties David's humbled state to the God who sees the affliction of His people, as He saw Israel's in Egypt, and answers it with mercy.

basic.context: David's flight continues, and along the way he meets two men from the house of Saul who reveal much about his humbled state. First is Ziba, Mephibosheth's servant, who brings generous provisions and then slanders his master, claiming Mephibosheth has stayed in Jerusalem hoping to reclaim Saul's throne. David, with no time to investigate, hastily grants Ziba all of Mephibosheth's property, a judgment he will have to revisit later. Then comes Shimei, a kinsman of Saul, who walks along cursing David, hurling stones and dust, and calling him a worthless man of blood who is now reaping God's judgment for the house of Saul. Abishai wants to behead him, but David restrains him with remarkable humility: perhaps the LORD has told Shimei to curse, and perhaps God will see David's affliction and repay him with good. So David absorbs the abuse and presses on, exhausted. Meanwhile Absalom enters Jerusalem in triumph. Hushai, David's secret agent, feigns loyalty to Absalom. And on Ahithophel's advice, Absalom publicly takes David's ten concubines on the palace roof, a brazen claim to the throne that fulfills, almost word for word, Nathan's judgment that David's wives would be taken in broad daylight. The chapter raises questions about bearing reproach humbly, discerning God's hand in suffering, and the sober unfolding of God's announced judgment.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative that interweaves David's humility with the outworking of God's judgment. David's restraint of Abishai models a striking submission to God's providence even in unjust abuse, though his hasty verdict on Mephibosheth also shows he is not infallible. The statement that the LORD 'told' Shimei to curse should be read within David's humble uncertainty ('if,' 'perhaps'), affirming God's overarching sovereignty without excusing Shimei's malice, which David later still judges. The public violation of the concubines is reported as the fulfillment of Nathan's word and the fruit of Ahithophel's wicked counsel, not endorsed.
basic.originalLanguages: Shimei relentlessly qalal, curses, David, treating the LORD's anointed as worthless, a grave act that David nonetheless refuses to avenge. Instead David hopes that the LORD will look on his oni, his affliction, the humiliation of the lowly, and repay him with good. The two words frame David's posture: reviled and pelted, he neither retaliates nor despairs, but entrusts his humbled state to the God who sees affliction and answers it with mercy.
basic.typology: David, the anointed king unjustly reviled as a man of blood, bearing curses and stones without retaliation and entrusting himself to God, foreshadows Christ, who was reviled and reviled not in return, who bore false accusation in silence, and who committed Himself to the Father who judges justly. David's hope that God would see his affliction and repay good anticipates the vindication God gave His suffering Son.
basic.christ: David reviled yet not retaliating points directly to Christ. When Shimei curses and stones him, David forbids vengeance and hopes for God's mercy; when Christ was cursed, mocked, and struck, He did not retaliate but entrusted Himself to the Father, and God repaid His affliction with the good of resurrection and exaltation. David is falsely called a man of blood; Christ, truly innocent, was numbered with transgressors. The suffering king who bears reproach and trusts God is fulfilled in the suffering Servant.
basic.god: God is the one David sees behind even Shimei's cursing, so that David bows to God's providence rather than lashing out, trusting that the LORD who ordains his affliction may yet repay him with good. God is also the one whose word through Nathan is now being fulfilled in Absalom's public sin, showing that God's announced judgments come to pass. Thus God is revealed as sovereign over both the abuse David suffers and the consequences of David's own past sin, and as the God who sees affliction and answers it.
basic.crossReferences: Second Samuel 12 records Nathan's prophecy, now fulfilled, that David's wives would be taken in broad daylight. First Peter 2 presents Christ, who when reviled did not revile in return but entrusted Himself to God. Second Samuel 19 tells how David later spares and then, through Solomon, judges Shimei. And Romans 12 counsels leaving vengeance to God, as David does here.
basic.oneStory: At his lowest, the anointed king bears cursing and reproach without retaliation, entrusting his affliction to God, while God's word of judgment is fulfilled through Absalom's brazen sin. This humbled, reviled king who will not avenge himself but hopes in God points forward to Jesus, the truly innocent King who bore reproach in silence and was vindicated by the Father who saw His affliction.

context.literary:
The chapter is built from three roadside or rooftop scenes that circle the same question, who really rules and by what right. Ziba and Shimei, verses 1 to 14, both belong to the house of Saul, and the narrator sets a giver beside a curser, a servant offering provisions and a kinsman offering stones, so that the reader must weigh two very different claims on David's favor within a dozen verses. The middle scene multiplies the verb qalal, curse, across verses 5, 7, 9, 10, 11, 12, and 13, an unusually heavy repetition that makes the abuse feel unrelenting even on the page, matched by a refrain of restraint, David's threefold 'leave him alone,' 'let him curse,' 'let him alone,' that answers each fresh insult without ever escalating.

David's rebuke of Abishai, 'what have I to do with you, O sons of Zeruiah,' verse 10, is not a new line but a deliberate echo of his own earlier refusal to let anyone harm Saul, 'who can lift a hand against the LORD's anointed and be guiltless,' 1 Samuel 26:9, and it will recur nearly verbatim when Abishai wants Shimei killed a second time, 2 Samuel 19:22. The repetition across three separate scenes, years apart, turns a passing remark into a settled conviction: David will not let vengeance be taken in his name, whether the anointed one at risk is Saul or, now, himself.

The final scene moves the action from the open road to a rooftop, a tent pitched in full public view, verse 22, a staging that answers, almost as a rhyme, the private rooftop where David's own great sin began, 2 Samuel 11:2. What David did in secret from a roof, the LORD had promised through Nathan would be answered in daylight, 2 Samuel 12:11 to 12, and the chapter closes by showing that promise fulfilled to the letter, on a roof again, before all Israel.
context.historical:
Bahurim, where Shimei meets David, was already a place marked by grief in this story; it is the very village where Michal's first husband Paltiel 'followed her, weeping all the way' before Abner sent him back, 2 Samuel 3:16, so David passes through ground already soaked in someone else's sorrow before adding his own. Throwing stones and flinging dust at a passing figure, verse 13, functioned as a public act of contempt and cursing in the ancient world, not mere annoyance, meant to be seen and reported, which is exactly why Shimei performs it 'along the ridge of the hill opposite,' in plain view of the whole company.

Ziba's report that Mephibosheth hoped Israel would 'restore to me the kingdom of my grandfather,' verse 3, exploits a real dynastic possibility; as Saul's surviving grandson, Mephibosheth was the one man in Israel with a plausible rival claim to the throne on genealogical grounds, which is what makes the slander credible enough for David to act on at once, without the leisure a calmer moment would have allowed for checking it.

Sleeping publicly with a former king's concubines, Ahithophel's counsel in verse 21, claimed the throne by a recognized custom rather than mere shock value; the same logic underlies Reuben's disqualifying act with his father's concubine, Genesis 35:22 and 49:4, and it is why Solomon later treats a simple request for his father's attendant Abishag as tantamount to a bid for the crown itself, 'you might as well request the kingdom for him,' 1 Kings 2:22. Absalom's public tent on the roof was therefore read by everyone watching as exactly what Ahithophel intended, an irreversible, unmistakable claim to David's throne.
context.canonical:
The chapter completes, almost word for word, the sentence Nathan pronounced years earlier, 'I will take your wives and give them to another, and he will lie with them in broad daylight... you have acted in secret, but I will do this thing in broad daylight before all Israel,' 2 Samuel 12:11 to 12; what was future judgment there becomes reported fact here, in the same city, on a rooftop that answers the rooftop where the original sin began, 2 Samuel 11:2.

David's restraint toward Shimei is not the end of that relationship. He later swears an oath sparing Shimei's life when the tables turn, 'you shall not die,' 2 Samuel 19:23, yet still remembers the cursing as unfinished business on his deathbed, instructing Solomon not to 'hold him guiltless,' 1 Kings 2:8 to 9, a charge Solomon eventually carries out, 1 Kings 2:36 to 46. Read across these three scenes, David's submission here in chapter 16 is shown to be neither denial that a wrong occurred nor a permanent amnesty, but a decision to leave the timing and manner of justice in God's hands rather than his own.

Ziba's slander against Mephibosheth is likewise not settled here; it is only in 2 Samuel 19:24 to 30 that Mephibosheth gets to answer for himself, revealing Ziba's deception and leaving David to split the difference in a ruling that satisfies no one fully, a reminder that this chapter's hurried verdict, verse 4, was provisional rather than final.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The author wants the reader positioned exactly where David is, hearing an accusation that is legally false in its specifics, David never shed Saul's blood or his house's, yet touches a real and deeper guilt, the blood of Uriah, so that Shimei's malice and Shimei's accuracy have to be held apart with care. The intent is not to vindicate Shimei's cruelty, which the narrator never softens, but to let David's own conscience, still tender from Nathan's rebuke, hear even a slanderous curse as possibly containing a splinter of truth he cannot simply dismiss. At the same time the author means to display, in Ziba's hasty reward and Absalom's brazen sin on the roof, how quickly a king under pressure can misjudge on partial evidence and how precisely God's own announced judgments arrive regardless. The chapter teaches, by showing rather than stating, that a person can be genuinely wronged, as David is by Shimei's cursing, and genuinely guilty, as David is before God, in the very same breath, and that only humility before God, not self justification, can hold those two truths together without collapsing into either denial or despair.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: David's hasty ruling in Ziba's favor, verse 4, is recorded, not commended; the narrator lets the reader watch a king act on one witness's word alone, in obvious haste, and then lets chapter 19 quietly correct the record, which is the Bible's own way of teaching, through consequence rather than commentary, that even a godly leader's snap judgments are not beyond error. Likewise Absalom's public claim on the concubines is reported as the fulfillment of a specific prophetic sentence, not as a model of anything, a warning against reading every fulfilled prediction as also an approved action. What is offered for imitation is narrower and more demanding: David's refusal to let personal insult be avenged by his own hand, choosing instead to entrust the outcome to a God who sees what he cannot yet see, a pattern of restraint the New Testament will commend explicitly rather than merely describe, and one a reader is meant to carry into ordinary reproach and betrayal long after Shimei's stones have been forgotten.

debates.question: In what sense had the LORD 'told' Shimei to curse David?

views.label: God's overruling sovereignty, not a command excusing Shimei
views.case: David speaks carefully, 'if the LORD told him,' and 'perhaps the LORD will repay me with good,' expressing humble submission to God's providence rather than a claim that God authored Shimei's malice; God sovereignly ordains that David face this reproach as part of his humbling and discipline, yet Shimei remains morally responsible, which is why David can still later regard his cursing as a real wrong, 1 Kings 2:8-9, so God's sovereignty and Shimei's guilt stand together.

views.label: David's faith reading God's discipline into his suffering
views.case: Others stress that David, chastened by his own sin, receives the cursing as part of God's just discipline and refuses to fight it, interpreting even an enemy's abuse as something God can use for his good; on this view David is not making a metaphysical claim about God commanding Shimei but humbly submitting to God's hand in the affliction, hoping for mercy.

debates.bearing: Both agree David bows to God's sovereign hand in his suffering without excusing Shimei's sin; the passage models humble submission to God's providence in the face of unjust reproach, entrusting vindication to the LORD who sees affliction, a posture perfected in Christ who when reviled did not revile in return.

debates.question: Was David right to grant Ziba all of Mephibosheth's property on the strength of a single, unverified accusation, verse 4?

views.label: An understandable, if imperfect, wartime decision
views.case: David is fleeing for his life with no time or means to summon Mephibosheth for a hearing, and Ziba arrives with tangible, needed provisions at the very moment the accusation is made, so a swift ruling, however incomplete the evidence, was a practical necessity of the crisis rather than a considered legal judgment meant to stand unquestioned.

views.label: A real and later corrected injustice
views.case: Mephibosheth is given no chance to answer at all, and when he finally does, 2 Samuel 19:24 to 30, his account of Ziba's deception is credible enough that David himself, by splitting the inheritance rather than restoring it fully, effectively admits his first ruling cannot simply stand; the text lets a reader see a real wrong done to a vulnerable man, lame from childhood and utterly dependent on David's earlier kindness, 2 Samuel 9.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree the verdict was made in haste on one sided testimony, and the narrative's own sequel treats it as needing correction rather than confirmation; the episode is a sober reminder that urgency and sincerity do not guarantee a right judgment, and that even a king famous for sparing his enemies can wrong a friend through simple carelessness.

study.originalLanguages:
Shimei's whole assault is carried by qalal, to curse, a root whose most basic sense is to be light, slight, or of little weight, the exact opposite of kabed, to be heavy, the same root that gives Hebrew its word for glory and honor. To curse someone in this vocabulary is, at the root, to declare them weightless, without honor, a fitting description of what Shimei is trying to do to the LORD's anointed with every stone and every shouted word, strip him publicly of the very kabod a king is due.

Against that assault David sets not a counter curse but oni, affliction, the word of the lowly and oppressed, 'perhaps the LORD will see my oni and repay me with good,' verse 12. The same word describes Hagar's suffering, answered by the LORD who 'heard your cry of affliction,' Genesis 16:11, and Israel's suffering in Egypt, 'I have indeed seen the affliction of My people,' Exodus 3:7. By reaching for this word rather than a plea for vindication or justice, David places himself, however briefly, among the categories of people Scripture consistently shows God noticing and answering, not the powerful demanding their rights but the afflicted hoping to be seen.

Abishai's insult, 'why should this dead dog curse my lord the king,' verse 9, borrows a set idiom that elsewhere works the opposite direction, as self deprecation rather than contempt for another; David calls himself 'a dead dog, a flea' before Saul, 1 Samuel 24:14, and Mephibosheth uses the identical phrase of himself before David, 'what is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog like me,' 2 Samuel 9:8. Abishai turns an idiom of humility into a weapon against someone else, which is itself a small but telling sign of how far his instinct runs from David's own, a king who has used that very phrase for himself but will not let it be hurled at an enemy in his name.

David's rebuke, 'what have I to do with you, O sons of Zeruiah,' verse 10, is not spontaneous but formulaic; the identical Hebrew idiom for rejecting someone's proposed course of action recurs at 2 Samuel 19:22 in almost the same words, a fixed phrase David reaches for whenever Joab's family wants blood he is not willing to authorize, whether the man at risk is Saul, years earlier, or, today, David's own tormentor.

typology.type: The anointed king cursed and pelted while his own armed men stand ready to strike back, verses 6 and 9
typology.fulfillment: David has 'the troops and all the mighty men' at hand and forbids them to act, verse 6, and 9 to 11. Jesus, arrested with a sword drawn in His defense, gives the same command, 'put your sword back in its place,' Matthew 26:52, refusing the legions of angels He could summon. Both kings possess the power to end the abuse instantly and both choose restraint, though David's is temporary submission within a story still unfolding and Christ's restraint carries Him all the way to the cross.

typology.type: A charge that is legally false yet touches a real, deeper guilt, verse 8
typology.fulfillment: Shimei's specific accusation, that David bears the blood of Saul's house, is untrue, yet it lands on a man who does carry real blood guilt of another kind, Uriah's. Christ bears the opposite pairing perfectly: 'He had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth,' Isaiah 53:9, wholly innocent of every charge yet 'numbered with the transgressors,' bearing guilt that was never His at all. The type is completed by contrast, a guilty man falsely accused giving way to an innocent one falsely condemned.

typology.type: Hope that God will see the affliction and repay it with good, verse 12
typology.fulfillment: David's tentative 'perhaps' becomes certainty in Christ, who endured the cross 'for the joy set before Him,' scorning its shame, and was seated at God's right hand, Hebrews 12:2, exalted by the Father precisely because He 'humbled Himself... to death, even death on a cross,' Philippians 2:8 to 9. What David can only hope for, Christ's story guarantees, affliction answered not merely with relief but with glory.

typology.type: The rooftop where the sin began answered by a rooftop where the sentence is carried out, 2 Samuel 11:2 and 16:22
typology.fulfillment: David's private sin on a rooftop is publicly judged on a rooftop, poetic justice within the same story. Christ's public shame on the cross works in the opposite direction, bearing a disgrace that is entirely undeserved so that guilty sinners might never have their own hidden sins publicly exposed and repaid in kind; where David's rooftop shame is corrective discipline for his own sin, Christ's public shame is substitutionary, absorbing what others deserved so that they need not.

study.christ:
David absorbing Shimei's curses without retaliation is one of the Old Testament's clearest previews of the Servant who would be reviled and not revile in return. Struck with stones and words, David forbids vengeance and simply endures, 'leave him alone and let him curse me, for the LORD has told him so,' verse 11; Jesus, cursed, mocked, and struck at His trial and crucifixion, 'did not retaliate; when He suffered, He made no threats, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23. The pattern is the same, endurance without reprisal, but the scale is not: David's silence spares his own dignity for a future vindication he can only hope for, while Christ's silence purchases the forgiveness of the very people cursing Him, so that on the cross He goes further than David ever does and prays for His accusers outright, 'Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,' Luke 23:34.

The charge against each king differs in exactly the way that matters most. Shimei calls David a man of blood, which is false as a specific charge about Saul's house yet uncomfortably close to David's true guilt over Uriah; Isaiah says of the Servant that He 'had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth,' Isaiah 53:9, a purity David could never claim for himself. David is a guilty man bearing an unjust accusation that nonetheless echoes a real fault; Christ is a wholly innocent man bearing an unjust accusation that echoes nothing true about Him at all, only the sin of those He came to save.

David's hope, 'perhaps the LORD will see my affliction and repay me with good,' verse 12, is answered for Christ not with a perhaps but with a certainty already secured before the affliction even began: He endured the cross 'for the joy set before Him,' Hebrews 12:2, and was 'highly exalted' precisely because He first humbled Himself to death, Philippians 2:8 to 9. What David can only hope his God will do, Christ's own resurrection and exaltation prove God has already determined to do for every affliction borne in trust, turning reproach itself into the road to glory.
study.god:
God's sovereignty in this chapter is exercised in a way that never removes moral responsibility from the people involved. David can say, 'if he curses me because the LORD told him, curse David, who can ask, why did you do this,' verse 10, without that sovereignty excusing Shimei, whom David still later calls to account, 1 Kings 2:8 to 9; the pattern matches the larger biblical witness that God can ordain that a trial befall His servant, as He permitted Satan to afflict Job, Job 1 to 2, without Himself becoming the author of the sin used to deliver it. God rules over the reproach without being its source.

God is also the one who sees what David, acting in haste, cannot yet see. He grants Ziba the whole of Mephibosheth's estate on a single unverified report, verse 4, a decision the following chapters will show to be at least partly mistaken; yet the God who truly knows the heart of both the slanderer and the slandered is not fooled even when His anointed king is, and Mephibosheth's vindication in chapter 19 belongs finally to Him, not to David's own discernment. The chapter thereby distinguishes what a king with partial information can judge from what only God, who sees completely, can judge rightly.

Above all, God is shown here as faithful to His own word regardless of how long it takes to come to pass. Absalom's brazen act on the rooftop fulfills, almost to the letter, a sentence God spoke through Nathan years earlier, 2 Samuel 12:11 to 12, and the precision of that fulfillment is itself a revelation of God's character, not vindictive but exact, a God whose announced judgments are never idle threats. For worship, the chapter teaches that the same God who sees the affliction of the falsely reviled also sees, and will eventually expose, every sin done in secret, so that both David's hope for mercy and Absalom's coming exposure rest on the same unwavering attribute of God, that He sees, and that what He has said will stand.

crossReferences.note: Nathan's specific sentence that David's wives would be taken 'in broad daylight' and 'before all Israel' is fulfilled almost verbatim when Absalom takes the concubines publicly on the roof, showing that God's announced judgments arrive with striking precision, however long delayed.

David's earlier refusal to let anyone 'lift a hand against the LORD's anointed' Saul supplies the exact conviction he now applies to himself, restraining Abishai from killing Shimei just as he once restrained him, and himself, from killing Saul.

David's own sin began on the roof of his palace, where he first saw Bathsheba; the concubines are violated on a roof as well, verse 22, a grim echo that ties the site of the original sin to the site of its public judgment.

The LORD's declaration that He has 'indeed seen the affliction' of His people in Egypt gives the same word, and the same divine attentiveness, that David hopes for when he asks the LORD to 'see my affliction' under Shimei's curses.

The Servant 'had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth,' the innocence Shimei's charge of bloodshed falsely denies David but which Christ, unlike David, actually possesses in full even while bearing the world's guilt.
Christ, reviled, did not revile in return but entrusted Himself to God who judges justly, the New Testament's own commentary on the posture David models under Shimei's stones and curses.

Paul's command to leave vengeance to God rather than avenging oneself is exactly what David practices by refusing Abishai's offer to kill Shimei, entrusting the wrong to the LORD's own justice instead.

Jesus goes beyond David's silent endurance to active intercession for His accusers, 'Father, forgive them,' the fullest possible answer to a reviled king's hope that God would somehow turn cursing into good.

David's deathbed instruction to Solomon shows that his restraint here was not a verdict that Shimei's cursing was harmless, only that vengeance was not David's to take in that hour; the debt is finally settled under Solomon.
Mephibosheth's own account exposes Ziba's slander as false, revising the hasty judgment of verse 4 and showing that David's swift ruling on the road was provisional, not the last word on the matter.

study.oneStory:
From the moment sin entered the world, the innocent and the guilty have often suffered side by side, and the wronged have had to decide whether to seize their own justice or wait for God's. This chapter sets that ancient choice before David in its starkest form: cursed publicly, pelted with stones, accused of a crime he did not commit while carrying the weight of one he did, he chooses neither denial nor retaliation but a bruised, waiting trust that God sees more than any human judge, including David himself, can see in the moment.

The chapter also shows redemption's story advancing exactly on schedule, however painful the timing. What Nathan spoke as future judgment over David's sin becomes present fact on Absalom's rooftop, proof within the story itself that God's word, once spoken, does not simply hang in the air waiting to be forgotten; it arrives, in its own time, with exactness. That same reliability is what allows David's hope in verse 12 to be more than wishful thinking, since the God who keeps His word of judgment can equally be trusted to keep His word of mercy.

What this chapter leaves incomplete, the rest of Scripture completes. David's restraint anticipates but does not equal the restraint of Jesus, who bears mockery that is wholly undeserved and answers it not with mere silence but with active forgiveness for those inflicting it. David's hope that God might repay affliction with good becomes, in Christ's resurrection and exaltation, a settled pattern for every sufferer who entrusts a reproach to God rather than avenging it personally.

The new creation finally closes the account this chapter opens. There every falsely accused servant of God is vindicated beyond doubt, every hidden sin already dealt with at the cross rather than waiting to surface in some future rooftop exposure, and 'they will reign forever and ever,' Revelation 22:5, no longer needing to hope, as David did, that God might see their affliction, but seeing His face and knowing, finally and fully, that He always did.

quiz.q: How does David respond when Shimei curses him and throws stones?

options.text: He forbids Abishai from killing Shimei, submitting to the possibility that the LORD is behind it and hoping God will repay him with good.
options.note: Verses 10-12 show David's humble restraint and trust rather than retaliation.

options.text: He orders his soldiers to seize and execute Shimei on the spot.
options.note: The opposite; David restrains Abishai from harming Shimei.

options.text: He restrains his men and bears the cursing without revenge.
options.note: True, but this option omits David's striking hope that the LORD may see his affliction and repay him with good.

options.text: He ignores Shimei entirely and says nothing about God's role.
options.note: David does speak, discerning God's hand in the cursing and hoping for His mercy, not merely ignoring it.

quiz.q: What does Absalom do on Ahithophel's advice, and what does it fulfill?

options.text: He publicly takes David's concubines on the palace roof, fulfilling Nathan's word that David's wives would be taken in broad daylight.
options.note: Verses 21-22 fulfill the judgment of 2 Samuel 12:11-12.

options.text: He simply moves into the palace and takes up residence quietly.
options.note: The act is a deliberate, public claim to the throne, not a quiet move, and it fulfills specific prophecy.

options.text: He seizes David's harem to claim the throne, as Ahithophel counseled.
options.note: True, but this option omits that it fulfills Nathan's specific prophecy of judgment on David.

options.text: He destroys the palace to erase David's memory.
options.note: He takes the concubines to claim the throne; he does not destroy the palace.

quiz.q: What does David hope for as he endures Shimei's cursing?

options.text: That the LORD will see his affliction and repay him with good for the cursing he receives.
options.note: Verse 12 records David's hope in God's mercy amid his humiliation.

options.text: That his soldiers will remember the insult and avenge it later.
options.note: David entrusts the matter to God, not to future vengeance by his men.

options.text: That God will notice his suffering and be gracious to him.
options.note: True, but this option omits the specific hope that God would repay good for the cursing itself.

options.text: That Shimei will repent and stop cursing him.
options.note: David's hope is in God's response to his affliction, not primarily in Shimei's repentance.

quiz.q: Why is David's hasty grant of Mephibosheth's property to Ziba noteworthy?

options.text: David acts on Ziba's one-sided slander without investigating, a rash judgment he will later have to revisit.
options.note: Verses 3-4 show David believing Ziba's accusation without hearing Mephibosheth, revisited in chapter 19.

options.text: It proves that David was always fair and never made mistakes in judgment.
options.note: The opposite; this is a rash, one-sided verdict, showing David is not infallible.

options.text: David believes Ziba's report too quickly and rules against Mephibosheth unheard.
options.note: True, but this option omits that David later has to reconsider the matter when he hears the other side.

options.text: David refuses Ziba's gift and reserves judgment until he returns.
options.note: David accepts the gift and grants Ziba the property immediately, rather than reserving judgment.

quiz.q: How does David's endurance of reproach point to Christ?

options.text: Reviled and not retaliating, entrusting his affliction to God, David foreshadows Christ who when reviled did not revile in return but trusted the Father.
options.note: David's restraint prefigures Christ, 1 Peter 2:23.

options.text: It teaches that God's king should always crush those who insult him.
options.note: David does the opposite, refusing vengeance, and Christ bore reviling in silence.

options.text: It models bearing insult without revenge, leaving vindication to God.
options.note: True, but this option omits the direct foreshadowing of Christ who committed Himself to the Father who judges justly.

options.text: It shows that suffering is always a sign of God's rejection.
options.note: David hopes God will repay good for his affliction; suffering here is discipline and testing, not rejection, and Christ's suffering led to glory.

questions: David bore Shimei's curses without striking back, wondering if God was even in it. When you are insulted or slandered, how do you respond, and could you entrust the matter to God instead of retaliating?
David hoped the LORD would see his affliction and repay him with good. Where in a current hardship do you need to hope that God sees and will bring good out of it?
David acted rashly on Ziba's one-sided report against Mephibosheth. Where are you at risk of judging a situation or a person on incomplete or slanted information?
Absalom's public sin fulfilled the exact judgment Nathan had spoken years earlier. How does the certainty that God's word comes to pass, in both warning and promise, shape the way you live now?
Christ bore reviling in silence and was vindicated by the Father. How does His example strengthen you to endure unfair treatment without bitterness or revenge?

translationNotes.note: David's words 'if the LORD told him, Curse David' express humble submission to God's sovereign providence in his suffering, not a claim that God authored Shimei's malice; David still later regards the cursing as a real wrong, 1 Kings 2:8-9.
The BSB footnote notes that some Septuagint manuscripts read the king 'arrived at the Jordan' exhausted, specifying the destination of this stage of David's flight.

Absalom's public taking of David's concubines on the roof deliberately fulfills Nathan's prophecy in 2 Samuel 12:11-12; the act is reported as the outworking of judgment and Ahithophel's wicked counsel, not as approved conduct.
